## Agenda 

-   Sampling theory: design vs. model-based\
-   Simulation framework\
-   Optimization criteria\

## 3. Why Sampling Matters

-   Limited resources → cannot measure entire population\
-   Need efficient, unbiased, precise estimates\
-   Choice of design strongly affects inference

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4. Common Sampling Strategies

-   Simple Random Sampling (SRS)\
-   Stratified Sampling\
-   Cluster Sampling\
-   Model/ML-informed Sampling

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Theory: Two Paradigms

-   **Design-based inference**\
-   **Model-based inference**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 6. Design-based Inference

-   Probability sampling\
-   Randomization ensures unbiasedness\
-   Variance estimated from design

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7. Model-based Inference

-   Assumes a stochastic model for population\
-   Efficiency from model assumptions\
-   Sensitive to misspecification

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 8. Monte Carlo Simulation

-   Framework for repeated sampling\
-   Generate many replications\
-   Assess bias, variance, MSE

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 9. Simulation-based Evaluation

-   Flexible and transparent\
-   Compare competing designs\
-   Helps optimize under constraints

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 10. Optimization Goals

-   **Minimize bias**\
-   **Minimize variance**\
-   **Control cost / feasibility**\
-   **Maximize precision**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 11. Bias vs. Variance Tradeoff

-   Small sample → high variance\
-   Complex model → possible bias\
-   Simulation helps balance

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 12. Workflow

1.  Generate synthetic population\
2.  Define sampling schemes\
3.  Draw repeated samples\
4.  Estimate parameter\
5.  Compute metrics

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 13. Metrics

-   **Bias**\
-   **Variance**\
-   **Mean Squared Error (MSE)**\
-   **Design Effect (DEFF)**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 14. Practical Session

We will use **R** to:\
- Simulate a population\
- Apply multiple sampling schemes\
- Evaluate metrics

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 15. R Setup

```{r}
set.seed(123)
N <- 10000
population <- data.frame(
  id = 1:N,
  x = rnorm(N, mean=50, sd=10),
  strata = sample(1:4, N, replace=TRUE),
  cluster = sample(1:200, N, replace=TRUE)
)
true_mean <- mean(population$x)
true_mean
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 16. Sampling Scheme: SRS

```{r}
sample_srs <- function(pop, n=200) {
  idx <- sample(pop$id, n)
  pop[idx,]
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 17. Sampling Scheme: Stratified

```{r}
sample_stratified <- function(pop, n=200) {
  split <- split(pop, pop$strata)
  sizes <- rep(n/length(split), length(split))
  do.call(rbind, Map(function(df, size) df[sample(nrow(df), size),], split, sizes))
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 18. Sampling Scheme: Cluster

```{r}
sample_cluster <- function(pop, n_clusters=10) {
  clusters <- sample(unique(pop$cluster), n_clusters)
  subset(pop, cluster %in% clusters)
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 19. Sampling Scheme: ML-informed

```{r}
## Assume probability proportional to x
sample_ml <- function(pop, n=200) {
  probs <- pop$x / sum(pop$x)
  idx <- sample(pop$id, n, prob=probs)
  pop[idx,]
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 20. Simulation Function

```{r}
simulate_design <- function(sampler, B=500, pop=population) {
  estimates <- replicate(B, {
    samp <- sampler(pop)
    mean(samp$x)
  })
  data.frame(
    mean_est = mean(estimates),
    bias = mean(estimates) - true_mean,
    var = var(estimates),
    mse = mean((estimates - true_mean)^2)
  )
}
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 21. Run Simulations

```{r}
results <- rbind(
  cbind(design="SRS", simulate_design(sample_srs)),
  cbind(design="Stratified", simulate_design(sample_stratified)),
  cbind(design="Cluster", simulate_design(sample_cluster)),
  cbind(design="ML-informed", simulate_design(sample_ml))
)
results
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 22. Design Effect

```{r}
results$deff <- results$var / results$var[results$design=="SRS"]
results
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 23. Visualization

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(results, aes(x=design, y=mse, fill=design)) +
  geom_col() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title="MSE by Sampling Design")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 24. Discussion

-   Trade-offs between designs\
-   Stratification often reduces variance\
-   Clustering may inflate variance\
-   ML-informed designs depend on model accuracy

------------------------------------------------------------------------

-   Simulation is powerful for evaluation\
-   Optimization balances bias, variance, cost\
-   R provides flexible tools\
